vignette:
Martin Keller, a 56-year-old white American musician, came to treatment after more than a year of living in an ever-shrinking world. He was married and had spent most of his adult life playing evening sets in bars, hotel lounges, and private events, the kind of work that put him in crowded rooms where people drank, moved unpredictably, and wore strong scents. The assault had happened after a late gig at a private club. He had been packing up when a man connected to the venue, someone with a confident, controlling manner, cornered him in a back room. What Martin remembers most sharply are fragments: the smell of the man's cologne when he was pinned close, a glimpse of blood after he was hurt, and the sudden violence of the man's movements. Other parts fall away entirely. Even now he cannot give a continuous account of what happened from beginning to end; as he gets near the missing parts, his mind seems to shut a door.

In the weeks after, Martin found that the broken quality of the memory seemed to make ordinary moments dangerous. The clear shards-cologne, blood, abrupt motion-stood out with a terrible force because they were not embedded in a story he could place in the past. A man brushing by him in a hallway wearing a similar scent, a split knuckle on someone loading equipment, even an argument breaking out near a stage could hit him with the same sick jolt, as if his body had recognized the event before his mind had. Because so much of the assault remained blank, he was left scanning for these bits in the present, trying to catch danger from clues he did not fully understand.

That vigilance hardened quickly. Martin had come to feel safe only at home, in one room with the door locked, or in the small studio where he practiced alone. Outside those places he was on edge, especially if someone moved suddenly beside him. In clubs and rehearsal spaces, when a stagehand reached across him without warning or a patron lurched too close after drinking, he was instantly braced, heart racing, shoulders set. He had become irritable in ways that startled him; small interruptions could bring a sharp, angry snap, and he hated that side of himself. The violence in the room around him, even raised voices or rough joking, now seemed to prove that threat was everywhere.

As that sense of danger grew, Martin began organizing his life around avoiding what set it off. He stopped taking bookings that involved security staff, police presence, or venue managers in uniforms, because being around authority figures made his whole body tighten. He no longer joined the other musicians for drinks after a set and gradually stopped seeing friends he had socialized with before the assault; they belonged to the old music scene, and returning to them felt too exposed. He also worked hard never to let himself feel angry. Anger felt perilous to him, too close to the violence of that night, so he pressed it down until it came out sideways as irritability at home. These habits cost him work and left his wife increasingly aware of how confined and defensive he had become.

His way of dealing with the memory only deepened its fractured quality. Whenever an image began to form, Martin cut it off before it could fully arrive. He would distract himself, leave the room, pick up his guitar and run scales, anything to stop the recollection before it gathered momentum. The result was that the assault remained a set of isolated flashes-one unbearably clear moment followed by blankness-rather than something he could think through. Because he never stayed with it long enough to make sense of it, he remained unable to tell himself a coherent story, and each return of the fragments felt raw and immediate rather than known.

The same avoidance fed the power of his triggers. By steering clear of old friends, certain venues, and anyone in authority, he never had a chance to test whether every cue meant danger now. A trace of cologne in an elevator, blood on a bandmate's finger during setup, or a scuffle outside a club door still landed with full force. And when those moments set off his alarm, the surge itself made the memory retreat again; he would feel the beginning of recognition, then clamp down, left only with the conviction that something terrible was about to happen. His wife finally urged him to seek help after he nearly walked out of a wedding performance when a guest in formalwear leaned in close, smelling of the same cologne, and another man made a sudden movement near the stage. Martin said what frightened him most was that his life had narrowed to a few safe places and a handful of rules, and even those no longer felt reliable. What he wanted, more than anything, was to be able to remember what happened without feeling that he was back there and to return to making music without bracing for danger in every room.
